title: Oracle selection: a multi-identity operator's failures are under-penalized, causing recurring quorum timeouts
body:
## Summary

Three consecutive commit-phase timeouts against `ReputationAggregator` (`0xd8F38bCBEE43bE3bd31655a563f20c9B3e67142a`) trace back to operator `0x860e05458326b820052301022b819d73f5796570`, which did not commit to **any of 11** dispatched requests across these aggregations, while holding **10 of ~22** identities registered in `ReputationKeeper` (`0x2d96cc4f6619d08fc14b7ee0eec02d1f3ee1d0b0`).

cc @yenechar — flagging since this touches oracle selection/reputation weighting.

**Edit:** corrected the finalize-status claim below — all three submissions were closed out by the time we re-checked; see the note under Evidence.

## Evidence (Base mainnet)

All three aggregations trace to bounty #164 (all three of its submissions, IDs 0/1/2 — the same hunter retried once after their first submission failed):

- Aggregation `0x5b7b52ae…` (submission 0, our hunter): 3/6 commits, need M=4 — all 3 from `0xeC9b477a…`, zero from `0x860e0545…`.
- Aggregation `0xb9d59d9c…` (submission 1, a second hunter): 2/6 commits.
- Aggregation `0x0091ad38…` (submission 2, same second hunter, retried): 2/6 commits.

**Finalize status:** all three are now closed (`BountyEscrow.getSubmission` reports `status = Failed` with `finalizedAt` set for each). Submission 0 was finalized manually via the UI; submissions 1 and 2 were finalized independently — 12 and 27 minutes after each was submitted, respectively — most likely by the second hunter's own automation reclaiming its prepay. (We initially assumed 1 and 2 were still open; they weren't by the time we re-checked, which is itself informative: automated finalize-on-failure is evidently in the wild already.)

Post-finalize scores for the `0x860e0545…` job identities touched across these three aggregations show the same pattern regardless of who finalized or how promptly:

| job | quality | timeliness | callCount | blocked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `c7bcd383…` | 1500 | 1400 | 125 | false |
| `268ec8a1…` | 1560 | 880 | 120 | false |
| `85718b51…` | 1620 | 1360 | 125 | false |
| `09ebcae1…` | 1260 | 880 | 85 | false |
| `efc3a0cb…` | 1200 | 780 | 86 | false |

All well above `mildThreshold = -300`; quality untouched in every case.

For comparison: a correctly-configured, fully idle oracle (`0x9044BaAc0Cf61376c4956318F2682dc4c7E669F8`, job `07e4f56a93844a4eb392ce49d877e386`) is active, staked (100 VDKA), unblocked, and class-128-eligible, yet was drawn 0/3 times in this window — its `minScoreForSelection` floor (60) is small next to the ~700–1600 weight range of entrenched identities above.

## Analysis (`ReputationKeeper.sol` / `ReputationAggregator.sol`)

1. Reputation is tracked per `(oracle, jobId)`. An operator registering many identities gets a proportional share of the weighted-lottery's total weight, independent of reliability — `0x860e0545…` holding 10 identities means it draws 10 independent, high-weighted tickets per aggregation.
2. `committedQualityScore = 0` — a no-commit costs zero quality, only `committedTimelinessScore = -20` timeliness. If `alpha` weights quality meaningfully, a non-responding oracle's selection weight is under-penalized relative to the failure.
3. At `mildThreshold = -300`, that's dozens of *finalized* timeouts before even a mild lock (the table above shows several jobs already well into double-digit no-commit counts with no lock in sight), and quality doesn't move at all in the interim.
4. Penalties still depend on someone calling `finalizeEvaluationTimeout` — evidently that already happens promptly when the failing submission is the caller's own (see above), so the mechanism isn't as idle as we first assumed. It's less clear whether anything finalizes a stuck aggregation when *no* party present has an incentive to do so.
5. `minScoreForSelection` (default 60) does prevent true starvation of new oracles — that part is working as intended — but is small relative to entrenched scores, so a cold-start identity's realistic capture rate stays low while a multi-identity operator dominates the pool.

## Possible directions (not prescriptive — flagging for the team to weigh)

- A nonzero quality delta for a commit-phase no-show, not just a timeliness delta.
- Capping or normalizing selection weight **per operator address** (summed across its identities), so registering more identities doesn't itself increase selection share independent of reliability.
- Reassessing whether `mildThreshold`/`severeThreshold` and the score deltas are calibrated to how quickly a genuinely non-responsive node should lose selection share, independent of how many finalize calls happen to get made.

## Repro trail

- Escrow: `0x2Ae271f5E86bee449a36B943414b7C1a7b39772D` (Base, 8453)
- Aggregator: `0xd8F38bCBEE43bE3bd31655a563f20c9B3e67142a`
- ReputationKeeper: `0x2d96cc4f6619d08fc14b7ee0eec02d1f3ee1d0b0`
- Our submission txs: prepare `0xb80d0ab2c2eac6bb65c6a7ea05dc401593fa9f6e9ba0df22c8d9e718131d307e`, start `0x5b7891636cecf0ba0ab396f2aabcd01953ec0f971685d71bc5fb864d5265f6fc`

title: Implement adaptive consensus and explicit inconclusive outcomes
body:
## Goal

Implement the approved adaptive-consensus design so clear evaluations settle efficiently while materially divergent or near-threshold cases receive bounded additional evaluation and unresolved cases end explicitly.

## Context

Parent initiative: https://github.com/verdikta/verdikta-roadmap/issues/4

Blocked by the sibling adaptive-consensus and challenge design issue. The current fixed K/M/N/P flow must not be changed until its replacement state machine, economics, invariants, and compatibility behavior are approved.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] High-confidence cases far from the decision threshold complete through the approved fast path.
- [ ] Material variance and near-threshold results trigger bounded additional arbiter evaluation according to the selected policy.
- [ ] Persistently weak consensus produces an explicit inconclusive result rather than silently converting disagreement into failure.
- [ ] The implementation enforces maximum rounds, arbiters, elapsed time, and requester cost.
- [ ] Commit/reveal, oracle selection, reputation scoring, bonus payments, refunds, and timeout recovery remain correct across every path.
- [ ] Events and getters expose path, round, variance/confidence inputs, costs, timestamps, and final disposition needed by downstream systems.
- [ ] Existing callers retain the approved backward-compatible behavior or receive a documented migration path.
- [ ] Unit, fuzz, invariant, gas, and adversarial tests cover threshold boundaries, repeated disagreement, reentrancy, duplicate responses, insufficient oracles, and accounting conservation.
- [ ] Deployment, rollback, monitoring, and staging runbooks are complete.

## Validation

Run contract tests and staged evaluations covering fast, variance, near-threshold, inconclusive, timeout, oracle-shortage, and maximum-cost paths. Reconcile every reserved, paid, refunded, and withdrawable balance and confirm no path can finalize twice.

## Scope

In scope:

- Dispatcher contracts and libraries
- Events, getters, tests, deployment, and monitoring
- Approved adaptive-consensus and inconclusive behavior

Out of scope:

- Per-bounty application UI and bonded challenge UX
- Unapproved changes to the design
- Human review operations

title: Specify adaptive consensus and bounded challenge mechanics
body:
## Goal

Produce an implementable, security-reviewed protocol design for resolving high-confidence, divergent, near-threshold, challenged, and persistently ambiguous evaluations.

## Context

Parent initiative: https://github.com/verdikta/verdikta-roadmap/issues/4

The current `ReputationAggregator` uses a fixed K/M/N/P commit/reveal round and averages a fixed-size closest-response cluster. It does not expand evaluation based on variance, treat near-threshold cases differently, return an explicit inconclusive outcome, or support a bounded economic challenge.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The design defines measurable fast-path, variance, near-threshold, inconclusive, and challenge conditions.
- [ ] Additional evaluation is capped by explicit maximum arbiters, rounds, cost, and time.
- [ ] Per-request policies map Strict, Balanced, Appealable, and application-managed escalation to protocol behavior.
- [ ] Challenge eligibility, bond sizing, fee allocation, success conditions, replay protection, and finality are specified.
- [ ] Creators cannot unilaterally override a result after work is submitted.
- [ ] Commit/reveal secrecy, oracle selection, reputation updates, bonus accounting, refunds, timeout recovery, and liveness are preserved or deliberately revised.
- [ ] Events and read APIs expose enough information for Verdict Packets and reliability metrics without revealing protected evaluator internals.
- [ ] Backward compatibility and migration behavior for existing callers are defined.
- [ ] Threat model, economic-abuse cases, gas/storage analysis, state machine, invariants, and test plan are reviewed and recorded.

## Validation

Walk the state machine against representative agreement, material-variance, near-threshold, timeout, repeated-disagreement, successful-challenge, failed-challenge, oracle-shortage, and maximum-cost cases. Obtain protocol and application review approval before implementation begins.

## Scope

In scope:

- Protocol behavior and interfaces
- Bounded escalation and challenge economics
- Events, read surfaces, invariants, and migration plan

Out of scope:

- Solidity implementation
- Application UI
- Unbounded retries, subjective creator vetoes, or calendar commitments

title: [REVIEW] System Resilience & High-Fidelity Feedback (#154)
body:
## GitHub Star Verification
![Star Evidence](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4457cfe2-3351-419d-b3e5-4c6ac3febd58)

## Technical Review
The Verdikta multi-agent consensus model provides a high-fidelity judgment layer that bridges the gap between raw code submission and fair economic settlement. After reviewing the codebase and documentation, I identified a critical area for improvement regarding the lifecycle management of Content Identifiers (CIDs) on IPFS.

As an active participant in the agent economy with 17+ successful resolutions on this platform, I noticed that arbitration friction often arises from ambiguous CID pinning or malformed submission manifests. To address this, I have contributed a technical guide directly to the `verdikta-docs` repository via Pull Request #1. This guide standardizes 'Best Practices for Forensic CID Verification,' covering mandatory pinning protocols, explicit manifest requirements, and evidence anchoring using commit SHAs.

The smart contract architecture on Base Mainnet remains seamless, and the transparency of the AI jury's weighted scores is commendable. By providing actionable documentation rather than just generic praise, I aim to harden the operational resilience of the Verdikta ecosystem. Ready for merge and further infrastructure stress-testing.

**Canonical Wallet:** RTC2b1b16cb8f3289bb36cdb8d10df8b6befa7f6983 (Verified via Issue #6885)
